entries.content_plain: PSALM 110 Psa 110:1-7 . The explicit application of this Psalm to our Saviour, by Him ( Mt 22:42-45 ) and by the apostles ( Ac 2:34 ; 1Co 15:25 ; He 1:13 ), and their frequent reference to its language and purport ( Ep 1:20-22 ; Php 2:9-11 ; He 10:12 , 13 ), leave no doubt of its purely prophetic character. Not only was there nothing in the position or character, personal or official, of David or any other descendant, to justify a reference to either, but utter severance from the royal office of all priestly functions (so clearly assigned the subject of this Psalm) positively forbids such a reference. The Psalm celebrates the exaltation of Christ to the throne of an eternal and increasing kingdom, and a perpetual priesthood ( Zec 6:13 ), involving the subjugation of His enemies and the multiplication of His subjects, and rendered infallibly certain by the word and oath of Almighty God. 1. The Lord said-- literally, "A saying of the Lord," (compare Psa 36:1 ), a formula, used in prophetic or other solemn or express declarations. my Lord-- That the Jews understood this term to denote the Messiah their traditions show, and Christ's mode of arguing on such an assumption ( Mt 22:44 ) also proves. Sit ... at my right hand-- not only a mark of honor ( 1Ki 2:19 ), but also implied participation of power ( Psa 45:9 ; Mr 16:19 ; Ep 1:20 ). Sit-- as a king ( Psa 29:10 ), though the position rather than posture is intimated (compare Ac 7:55 , 56 ). until I make, &c.-- The dominion of Christ over His enemies, as commissioned by God, and entrusted with all power ( Mt 28:18 ) for their subjugation, will assuredly be established ( 1Co 15:24-28 ). This is neither His government as God, nor that which, as the incarnate Saviour, He exercises over His people, of whom He will ever be Head. thine enemies thy footstool-- an expression taken from the custom of Eastern conquerors (compare Jos 10:24 ; Jud 1:7 ) to signify a complete subjection.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6806"/><div sID="gen10446" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6806"/><hi type="bold">2. the rod of thy strength--</hi>the rod of correction (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.4">Is 9:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.15">10:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.12">Jr 48:12</reference>), by which Thy strength will be known. This is His Word of truth (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.3">Is 2:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.4">11:4</reference>), converting some and confounding others (compare <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.8">2Th 2:8</reference>).<div eID="gen10446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10447" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">out of Zion--</hi>or, the Church, in which God dwells by His Spirit, as once by a visible symbol in the tabernacle on Zion (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Psa 2:6</reference>).<div eID="gen10447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10448" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rule thou, &c.--</hi>over enemies now conquered.<div eID="gen10448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10449" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the midst--</hi>once set upon, as by ferocious beasts (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.16">Psa 22:16</reference>), now humbly, though reluctantly, confessed as Lord (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.10">Php 2:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.11">11</reference>). <div eID="gen10449" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 2. the rod of thy strength-- the rod of correction ( Is 9:4 ; 10:15 ; Jr 48:12 ), by which Thy strength will be known. This is His Word of truth ( Is 2:3 ; 11:4 ), converting some and confounding others (compare 2Th 2:8 ). out of Zion-- or, the Church, in which God dwells by His Spirit, as once by a visible symbol in the tabernacle on Zion (compare Psa 2:6 ). rule thou, &c.-- over enemies now conquered. in the midst-- once set upon, as by ferocious beasts ( Psa 22:16 ), now humbly, though reluctantly, confessed as Lord ( Php 2:10 , 11 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6807"/><div sID="gen10450" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6807"/><hi type="bold">3. Thy people ... willing--</hi>literally, "Thy people (are) free will offerings"; for such is the proper rendering of the word "willing," which is a plural noun, and not an adjective (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.25.2">Ex 25:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.54.6">Psa 54:6</reference>), also a similar form (<reference osisRef="Judg.5.2-Judg.5.9">Jud 5:2-9</reference>).<div eID="gen10450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10451" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the day of thy power--</hi>Thy people freely offer themselves (<reference osisRef="Rom.12.1">Ro 12:1</reference>) in Thy service, enlisting under Thy banner.<div eID="gen10451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10452" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the beauties of holiness--</hi>either as in <reference osisRef="Ps.29.2">Psa 29:2</reference>, the loveliness of a spiritual worship, of which the temple service, in all its material splendors, was but a type; or more probably, the appearance of the worshippers, who, in this spiritual kingdom, are a nation of kings and priests (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.9">1Pe 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.5">Re 1:5</reference>), attending this Priest and King, clothed in those eminent graces which the beautiful vestments of the Aaronic priests (<reference osisRef="Lev.16.4">Le 16:4</reference>) typified. The last very obscure clause--<div eID="gen10452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10453" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from the womb ... youth--</hi>may, according to this view, be thus explained: The word "youth" denotes a period of life distinguished for strength and activity (compare <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.9">Ec 11:9</reference>)--the "dew" is a constant emblem of whatever is refreshing and strengthening (<reference osisRef="Prov.19.12">Pr 19:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.14.5">Ho 14:5</reference>). The Messiah, then, as leading His people, is represented as continually in the vigor of youth, refreshed and strengthened by the early dew of God's grace and Spirit. Thus the phrase corresponds as a member of a parallelism with "the day of thy power" in the first clause. "In the beauties of holiness" belongs to this latter clause, corresponding to "Thy people" in the first, and the colon after "morning" is omitted. Others prefer: Thy youth, or youthful vigor, or body, shall be constantly refreshed by successive accessions of people as dew from the early morning; and this accords with the New Testament idea that the Church is Christ's body (compare <reference osisRef="Mic.5.7">Mi 5:7</reference>). <div eID="gen10453" type="x-p"/>
